title: Private capital to drive 30 GW of India's 100 GW nuclear target by 2047
excerpt: Atomic Energy Commission chairman A K Mohanty said opening the nuclear sector to private players could draw ₹7.5 lakh crore in investment, as India targets about 22 GW by 2031-32 under its Nuclear Energy Mission.
body:
• Atomic Energy Commission chairman A K Mohanty said opening the nuclear sector to private players could draw ₹7.5 lakh crore in investment, with private firms contributing 30 GW toward India's 100 GW nuclear capacity target by 2047, according to a PTI report.
  • India's installed nuclear capacity stands at 8.78 GW from 24 reactors today; the government targets about 22 GW by 2031-32, with state-run NPCIL alone slated to reach 54 GW by 2047.
  • Mohanty said India holds 25 per cent of global thorium reserves, which will support the second and third stages of the country's three-stage nuclear programme, alongside 439,800 tonnes of identified in-situ uranium oxide resources.
  • What it means for you: the SHANTI Act has opened nuclear power to private capital for the first time. Watch for the final rules (public consultation on the draft began August 17) and upcoming NPCIL and private-sector tenders — the first real chance for investors to take exposure to India's atomic build-out. There is no near-term change to power tariffs; this is a multi-decade capacity programme.

India is opening its civil nuclear sector to private capital, with the government projecting that private players could invest up to ₹7.5 lakh crore and contribute 30 GW toward the country's goal of 100 GW of nuclear power capacity by 2047. The figures were shared by Atomic Energy Commission chairman A K Mohanty, according to a report by news agency PTI, in what amounts to the clearest quantification yet of the private-sector role in India's atomic ambitions.

The announcement marks the next step in a policy overhaul that has gathered pace this year. Until recently, nuclear power generation in India was the exclusive domain of state-run Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited (NPCIL), with a handful of public-sector joint ventures at the margins.

Context & Background

The groundwork for private entry was laid when the government launched the Nuclear Energy Mission for Viksit Bharat in January 2025, targeting 100 GW of nuclear capacity by 2047. In December 2025, Parliament passed the SHANTI Act, which opened the country's civil nuclear sector to private participation and modernised the legal framework governing it.

The Department of Atomic Energy opened public consultation on the SHANTI Act's draft rules on August 17, 2026. In a September statement at the IAEA's 69th General Conference, Mohanty said the government had allocated more than USD 2 billion for R&D on small modular reactors, with at least five indigenous SMRs to be operational by 2033. Mohanty has also held talks with US Energy Secretary Chris Wright in Washington to deepen Indo-US civil nuclear cooperation, as American and Canadian reactor makers eye the new market.

Impact & Analysis

The numbers spell out an enormous build-out. From 8.78 GW today — generated by 24 reactors — India must reach roughly 22 GW by 2031-32 and then climb more than fourfold to 100 GW by 2047. NPCIL is expected to reach 54 GW on its own by 2047, while other public-sector companies, state governments and private players contribute the remaining 46 GW, with the private sector accounting for 30 GW of that.

Thorium is central to the long-term strategy. The Department of Atomic Energy reports 1.18 million tonnes of thorium oxide resources in monazite deposits across coastal and inland states, plus about 439,800 tonnes of in-situ uranium oxide resources across eleven states from Andhra Pradesh to Maharashtra. India's three-stage nuclear programme is designed to make optimal use of limited uranium and harness thorium — which must first be converted into fissile uranium-233 before use as fuel — for long-term energy security.

The expansion is aimed at meeting rising electricity demand, strengthening energy security and diversifying the power mix with reliable, low-carbon generation — a role solar and wind cannot fully play given their intermittency.

Diaspora Angle

For diaspora investors, nuclear energy is becoming an investable theme in India for the first time, as private companies — including listed engineering and power firms — begin to enter a sector long closed to them. The Indo-US civil nuclear talks also matter: with Washington and New Delhi working to convert the new legal framework into commercial partnerships, American and Canadian companies are expected to compete for reactor, component and EPC contracts in the Indian market.

What's Next

The immediate milestone is the finalisation of the SHANTI Act's rules, now out for public consultation, which will define exactly how private players can participate — including liability, licensing and joint-venture structures. Watch for private announcements of nuclear tie-ups and NPCIL's capacity tenders, progress toward the 2031-32 goal of 22 GW, and the rollout of India's first indigenous SMRs toward the 2033 target. Further India-US engagement on civil nuclear cooperation is also expected to deepen in the coming months.
